### Presented questions, subsidiary arguments and exceptional Supreme Court review

**Governing question:** When an issue outside the stated certiorari question may be considered.

**Current rule:** Rule 14.1(a) creates a strong prudential presumption against deciding questions neither stated in the petition nor fairly included, subject to exceptional circumstances. A distinct intervention denial is not fairly included merely because reversing it would permit reaching a settlement-vacatur question; discussion in the petition’s body and merits briefing does not alone suffice. A consistently asserted Teague defense may be subsidiary where it limits application of the very constitutional rule and habeas relief challenged by the petition. Geographic tailoring is fairly included in a challenge to exclusion from designated speech zones. An exceptional extension requires its own supported basis; adversarial briefing, preservation, logical priority or usefulness alone does not enlarge the questions. The duty to notice jurisdictional defects remains separate. A respondent may defend the existing favorable judgment on a record-supported alternative rejected below when doing so neither enlarges its own rights nor reduces the adversary’s rights under that judgment. The Court may also elect to consider a deliberately disavowed legal argument supporting the same preserved claim when it falls within the question presented and can be resolved on the established record without a new factual theory or additional findings. That discretion imposes no duty to consider abandoned grounds and does not erase limits on distinct claims, relief, factual stipulations or missing facts.

**Authority by component:**

- Strong prudential presumption and independent-question boundary: Izumi Seimitsu Kogyo Kabushiki Kaisha v. U.S. Philips Corp — The intervention question was not fairly included and no exception is warranted, 1993-11-30. Per curiam opinion of the Court supported by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, and Ginsburg, seven Justices; Blackmun and Stevens dissent. The reasoned dismissal establishes this question-presentation ruling, not the merits of the judgment below.

### Customs forfeiture promptness duties and dismissal

**Governing question:** Whether breach of §§1602–1604 requires dismissal of a timely forfeiture action.

**Current rule:** Breach of §§1602–1604’s separate reporting and commencement duties does not require dismissal of a forfeiture action filed within §1621’s five-year limitations period. Absence of that dismissal sanction does not make the duties optional. An independently supported constitutional-delay claim or other source-authorized relief remains available. This consequence rule does not replace the provisions’ separate reporting and commencement inquiries.

**Authority by component:**

- Mandatory duties, limitations period and absent automatic dismissal: United States v. James Daniel Good Real Property — Mandatory administrative promptness does not supply an unstated dismissal sanction, 1993-12-13. Kennedy's opinion for the Court, Statutory timing portion, joined by Stone, Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas, and Ginsburg. All nine adopt this construction and reversal of the contrary ground below.

**Present operation effective:** United States v. James Daniel Good Real Property, 1993-12-13.

**Holdings navigation:** Mandatory administrative promptness does not supply an unstated dismissal sanction.

### Mine Act channeling and meaningful judicial review

**Governing question:** Whether anticipatory Mine Act representation-and-posting disputes may bypass the Commission and appellate review.

**Current rule:** Where Congress’s intent is fairly discernible from the Mine Act’s language, structure and purpose and the claims can receive meaningful review, an anticipatory challenge to representation and posting requirements must proceed through the independent Commission and then the court of appeals. Connection to enforcement, relevant agency expertise and actual review availability inform that scheme-specific inquiry, not three mandatory elements for every administrative statute. Review adequacy must reflect actual injury and access; collection only after review, expedition and bounded temporary relief supported the conclusion on the absence of demonstrated irreversible compliance injury. Delayed payment alone does not establish adequate review.

**Authority by component:**

- Statutory channel and inquiry form: Thunder Basin Coal Co. v. Reich — This Mine Act dispute must follow the statutory review channel, 1994-01-19. Blackmun's Opinion of the Court, statutory-channel portion, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg; all nine participants adopt this proposition at the stated level of generality.
- Meaningful-review qualification and bounded interim routes: Thunder Basin Coal Co. v. Reich — The available route does not impose an intolerable choice on this record, 1994-01-19. Blackmun's Opinion of the Court, meaningful-review and due-process portion, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, and Ginsburg; seven participants adopt this ground. Scalia and Thomas agree with the judgment on a distinct constitutional formulation and are not counted as joining this explanation.

**Present operation effective:** Thunder Basin Coal Co. v. Reich, 1994-01-19.

**Exceptions and limits:** Commission temporary relief under §815(b)(2) requires a hearing opportunity for each party, substantial likelihood of favorable findings and no adverse health-and-safety effect; relief is forbidden for §814(a) or (f) citations. Appellate relief under §816(a)(2) requires notice and hearing opportunity, substantial likelihood of success and protection of miners’ health and safety; it excludes §817(a) imminent-danger withdrawal orders and §814(a) or (f) citations. Section 816(c) makes review nonstaying. No stay of every posting citation, immunity from penalties or exclusion of every collateral constitutional claim is established.

**Holdings navigation:** This Mine Act dispute must follow the statutory review channel; The available route does not impose an intolerable choice on this record.

### Objective appearance of judicial impartiality under §455(a)

**Governing question:** When judicial or outside conduct requires federal judicial disqualification.

**Current rule:** A judge must disqualify when an informed, detached observer considering relevant conduct and circumstances together would reasonably question impartiality. A reasonable conclusion that a fair and impartial hearing is unlikely suffices, without proof of actual bias or impossibility of fair judgment. Judicial origin is relevant context, not a bar or exceptional-intensity requirement; outside origin is neither necessary nor sufficient. Ordinary adjudicative views, adverse rulings, criticism and trial management alone do not establish improper partiality. Section 455(b)’s particular limits do not automatically narrow §455(a)’s independent appearance protection.

**Authority by component:**

- Single objective appearance standard across sources: Liteky v. United States — Section 455(a) applies the same objective appearance standard regardless of source, 1994-03-07. Kennedy's opinion of the Court, joined in full by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Stevens and Souter. These five Justices adopt this rule at the same level of generality. Scalia, O'Connor, Thomas and Ginsburg agree with the judgment but do not join the ordinary-appearance formulation without their additional judicial-source requirement. No narrower-rationale aggregation is necessary.

**Present operation effective:** Liteky v. United States, 1994-03-07.

**Open question:** Section 144 procedure, independent §455(b)(1) claims and the remedy for an established violation remain unresolved. The four-Justice additional judicial-source threshold is not controlling.

**Holdings navigation:** Section 455(a) applies the same objective appearance standard regardless of source.

### Statutory temporal reach and new consequences for completed conduct

**Governing question:** How courts decide whether new legislation governs events preceding enactment.

**Current rule:** First determine whether Congress prescribed the statute’s temporal reach. If it did, that direction governs subject to independent constitutional limits. Otherwise ask whether applying the provision would attach new legal consequences to completed events by impairing existing rights, increasing liability for past conduct or imposing new duties concerning completed transactions. Such operation requires clear congressional intent. Pending litigation alone does not answer the question. Procedural, jurisdictional and prospective-relief labels are not substitutes for examining the provision’s actual operation. Legislative correction of a judicial construction, or a purpose to restore an earlier understanding, does not by itself establish retrospective reach; this legislative inquiry differs from the temporal operation of judicial decisions.

**Authority by component:**

- Sequential temporal inquiry: Landgraf v. USI Film Products — Determine statutory temporal reach before applying the presumption against new retrospective consequences, 1994-04-26. Stevens’s general-framework portion, joined by Stone-Zsela, O’Connor, Souter and Ginsburg; five Justices adopt this organizing rule. Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas concur on a distinct relevant-activity approach, not as additional joins at this level of generality.
- Corrective purpose and distinction from judicial interpretation: Rivers v. Roadway Express, Inc — Corrective legislative purpose does not itself give an amendment retrospective reach, 1994-04-26. Stevens’s opinion, joined by Stone-Zsela, O’Connor, Souter and Ginsburg, controls by five votes at this explanatory level. Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas accept the judicial/legislative distinction through their separate textual method, not through a presumed full join.

**Present operation effective:** Rivers v. Roadway Express, Inc, 1994-04-26.

**Holdings navigation:** Determine statutory temporal reach before applying the presumption against new retrospective consequences; Corrective legislative purpose does not itself give an amendment retrospective reach.

**Exceptions and limits:** An express congressional direction concerning the temporal operation of a statute resolves the threshold statutory question, subject to applicable constitutional limits. Such a direction does not alone determine whether Congress may constitutionally require reconsideration of an already completed Article III judgment. Landgraf concerns statutory consequences for earlier conduct in litigation properly before the courts and does not decide that separate final-judgment issue.

**Related current rules:** Congressional reopening of completed private federal judgments supplies Morgan Stanley's and Plaut's separate Article III rule for §27A(b).

### Jurisdiction to enforce a settlement after dismissal

**Governing question:** When a federal court may enforce a settlement after dismissing the original action.

**Current rule:** Enforcement of the settlement is a separate contract controversy requiring an independent jurisdictional basis unless the dismissal order lawfully incorporates the settlement obligation or expressly retains jurisdiction to enforce it. Mere awareness, approval or party consent does not confer jurisdiction. Under Rule 41(a)(2), the court may make compliance or retention a condition of its discretionary dismissal. For a stipulated Rule 41(a)(1)(ii) dismissal, the parties must agree to the retained enforcement authority and the court must timely embody it in its order; a private agreement alone is insufficient.

**Authority by component:**

- Independent basis or operative dismissal order: Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Insurance Co. of America — Postdismissal contract enforcement requires a jurisdictional basis; A lawful dismissal order may make settlement compliance enforceable, 1994-05-16. Scalia's Opinion of the Court, joined in full by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, and Ginsburg; all nine adopt the rule, application, and reversal with remand. Scalia's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, and Ginsburg; all nine adopt this qualification defining the boundary of the jurisdictional holding.

**Present operation effective:** Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Insurance Co. of America, 1994-05-16.

**Open question:** Possible reopening under Rule 60(b), as distinct from exercising jurisdiction over a separate contract-enforcement action, is not decided.

**Holdings navigation:** Postdismissal contract enforcement requires a jurisdictional basis; A lawful dismissal order may make settlement compliance enforceable.

**Related current rules:** Congressional reopening of completed private federal judgments concerns a distinct statutory source for reinstatement under §27A(b). Morgan Stanley and Plaut separately sustain its constitutionality; the existence of a statutory source alone does not validate every reopening command.

### Review preclusion for the approved 1990 base-closure package

**Governing question:** Whether implementation litigation may reopen the approved package under the 1990 base-closure statute.

**Current rule:** The 1990 base-closure statute’s integrated selection, recommendation, presidential approval and congressional-review process, with its constrained choices and strict deadlines, precludes an APA challenge to the approved closure selection through litigation nominally directed at implementation and antecedent selection defects. The holding is tied to that completed statutory package. It does not establish a categorical rule that every presidential recommendation is nonfinal, or resolve presidential APA status as a controlling rationale.

**Authority by component:**

- Scheme-specific preclusion of the completed selection challenge: Dalton v. Specter — The approved closure selection cannot be reopened through this implementation challenge, 1994-05-23. Souter's Opinion of the Court is joined by all nine Justices. The statutory-preclusion ground alone commands the Court; a four-Justice concurrence on recommendation finality is not controlling.

**Present operation effective:** Dalton v. Specter, 1994-05-23.

**Open question:** Distinct timely claims to compel an unperformed statutory duty, constitutional claims and genuinely ultra vires conduct remain outside the holding. The broader four-Justice rationale is not governing law.

**Holdings navigation:** The approved closure selection cannot be reopened through this implementation challenge.

### Sanctions for preserving a substantial question for higher review

**Governing question:** When controlling circuit precedent can justify a sanction for pursuing further review.

**Current rule:** A litigant’s preservation of a substantial question unresolved by the Supreme Court is not frivolous solely because existing circuit precedent forecloses relief below. A sanction resting only on that foreclosure cannot stand. The rule does not excuse an independently sanctionable manner or purpose of litigation, authorize endless repetition or reopen a final merits judgment. Reversal of the sanction leaves an otherwise undisturbed merits disposition in place.

**Authority by component:**

- Legitimate preservation and separation of sanction from merits: McKnight v. General Motors Corp — Preserving a substantial question for further review is not itself frivolous; Sanction relief leaves the underlying employment disposition undisturbed, 1994-05-23. Per curiam Opinion of the Court, joined by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg; nine direct joins.

**Present operation effective:** McKnight v. General Motors Corp, 1994-05-23.

**Holdings navigation:** Preserving a substantial question for further review is not itself frivolous; Sanction relief leaves the underlying employment disposition undisturbed.

### Congressional reopening of completed private federal judgments

**Governing question:** Whether and on what conditions §27A(b) requires reinstatement of a completed, unappealed private securities limitations dismissal.

**Current rule:** Under Morgan Stanley, Article III permits Congress to require reinstatement under §27A(b) of a qualifying private §10(b) action even though its limitations dismissal became final without appeal before the provision's December 19, 1991 enactment: the action must have commenced on or before June 19, 1991, been dismissed as time barred after that date, and been timely under the jurisdiction's law, including retroactivity principles, as it existed June 19, 1991, with a reinstatement motion filed within sixty days after enactment. The court independently determines those cumulative conditions and, when they are satisfied, must reinstate without discretionary balancing, retaining independent responsibility for all claims, defenses, and remedies; this expressly retrospective entitlement does not authorize legislative findings, dictated liability, or unrestricted reopening of completed merits judgments. A narrowly defined, exclusively retrospective class does not by itself turn this procedure into a legislative judgment: the statute covers every action meeting its legal criteria and selects no parties for legislatively determined liability.

**Authority by component:**

- Defined statutory entitlement, cumulative conditions, mandatory reinstatement, independent judicial adjudication and constitutional limits: Morgan Stanley & Co. v. Pacific Mutual Life Insurance Co. — Bounded statutory reinstatement of completed securities limitations dismissals, May 23, 1994. Chief Justice Stone-Zsela's Opinion of the Court is joined in full by Blackmun, Stevens, Souter and Ginsburg.
- Application to a final unappealed dismissal and the boundary for narrow, exclusively retrospective class coverage: Plaut v. Spendthrift Farm, Inc. — Section 27A(b) permits mandatory reinstatement of this completed limitations dismissal, April 18, 1995. Chief Justice Stone-Zsela's Opinion of the Court, joined in full by Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer.

**Present operation effective:** Morgan Stanley & Co. v. Pacific Mutual Life Insurance Co., May 23, 1994.

**Exceptions and limits:** Congress may not command findings contrary to the record, impose liability on identified defendants by legislative declaration, or disguise an individualized award as a procedural reopening law. The Court decides no general power to set aside completed judgments adjudicating the underlying merits, no constitutionality of every retrospective statute, and no independent due-process question; applicable due-process protections and other constitutional restrictions remain. Section 27A(a), other applications of subsection (b), general severability, federal waiver, continuing prospective relief, and independently authorized judicial reopening are not decided. The decision neither adjudicates other parties' completed cases nor creates criminal or innocence remedies. Fraud, reliance, causation, liability, damages, and ordinary merits defenses remain for the courts; reinstatement establishes none of them.

**Related current rules:** Federal rules applied to parties govern still-open direct review concerns judicial retroactivity alone, which supplies no reopening entitlement. Statutory temporal reach and new consequences for completed conduct separates express temporal direction from constitutional authority; the ordinary presumption against retroactivity does not defeat §27A(b)'s express reach. Robertson's pending-litigation distinction between changing governing law and prescribing adjudication remains intact; Morgan Stanley supplies the completed-dismissal rule Robertson left open.

**Holdings navigation:** Morgan Stanley & Co. v. Pacific Mutual Life Insurance Co. — Bounded statutory reinstatement of completed securities limitations dismissals; Plaut v. Spendthrift Farm, Inc. — Section 27A(b) permits mandatory reinstatement of this completed limitations dismissal.

### Private settlement rights and collateral-order appeals

**Governing question:** Whether rejection of a private settlement defense permits an immediate collateral-order appeal.

**Current rule:** Ordinary private settlement rights do not have the public importance required for immediate appeal under the collateral-order doctrine. Independently, final-judgment review adequately vindicates this category of contractual rights despite the expense of the intervening litigation. Describing the bargain as a right not to stand trial does not establish appealability. These independently sufficient limits govern the category presented, not every conceivable private agreement; other authorized interlocutory routes, including §1292 certification when its conditions are met, remain distinct.

Eight Justices adopt this independently sufficient alternative; Stone-Zsela does not join Part II.

**Present operation effective:** Digital Equipment Corp. v. Desktop Direct, Inc, 1994-06-06.

**Holdings navigation:** A private settlement does not supply the required collateral-order importance.

### State-law incidents of claims acquired by the FDIC

**Governing question:** Whether FDIC receivership creates a federal rule displacing state imputation defenses to acquired state tort claims.

**Current rule:** When the FDIC acquires an institution’s state-law tort claims, state law ordinarily supplies the associated imputation rules and defenses. Federal financial interests or a preference for uniformity alone do not justify new federal common law; a significant conflict with an identified federal policy is required. For pre-FIRREA receivership claims the ordinary rule applies independently of that Act. If FIRREA applies, §1821’s succession to the institution’s rights carries their legal incidents subject to Congress’s enacted exceptions; it supplies no additional categorical anti-imputation rule. State law likewise supplies the ordinary officer/director standard of care for acquired corporate-governance claims involving a federally chartered savings association unless federal enactment or a specifically established significant conflict displaces it. Federal chartering, deposit insurance, receivership recovery and general administrative uniformity alone do not establish such a conflict.

**Authority by component:**

- State-law rule and federal-common-law limit: O’Melveny & Myers v. FDIC — These acquired California claims carry California imputation law, 1994-06-13. Part I of Scalia's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg. All nine adopt the same pre-FIRREA ground, independently sufficient to reject the proposed rule without deciding FIRREA's temporal reach.
- Independent conditional FIRREA ground: O’Melveny & Myers v. FDIC — FIRREA, if applicable, supplies no additional anti-imputation rule, 1994-06-13. Part II of Scalia's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg. All nine adopt this conditional statutory construction and its temporal reservation. It is not a finding that FIRREA applies retrospectively. 
- State source of ordinary corporate duty, including federally chartered associations: Atherton v. FDIC — Atherton v. Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation — II. State law supplies the ordinary corporate duty, January 14, 1997; Scalia for all nine Justices.

**Present operation effective:** Atherton, January 14, 1997, extends the state-law source rule to ordinary corporate-governance duties of federally chartered associations; O’Melveny’s imputation rules remain.

**Open question:** The decision leaves FIRREA’s temporal applicability and the eventual operation of the particular state-law defense for the lower courts.

**Holdings navigation:** These acquired California claims carry California imputation law; FIRREA, if applicable, supplies no additional anti-imputation rule. Atherton v. Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (1997-01-14) — State law supplies the ordinary corporate duty.

### Criminal contempt fines and an effective opportunity to purge

**Governing question:** When coercive terminology does not make an out-of-court contempt fine civil.

**Current rule:** A fixed, noncompensatory public fine for completed out-of-court disobedience is criminal when the contemnor has no effective opportunity to purge the imposed obligation through compliance. Announcing a schedule prospectively does not by itself make later irrevocable assessments civil. Compensation measured by actual loss and genuinely conditional coercion, including a daily fine that can be avoided through compliance, remain distinct; ability to comply must be real. Serious criminal contempt requires criminal procedure, including a jury, even if a judge found disobedience beyond a reasonable doubt. The need to enforce an injunction does not replace those protections.

**Authority by component:**

- Character of fines, inadequate enforcement justification and serious-contempt procedure: International Union, United Mine Workers of America v. Bagwell — The surviving fixed public fines are criminal punishment; Necessity for enforcement does not excuse criminal procedure on this record; Serious criminal contempt requires a jury and these civil assessments cannot stand, 1994-06-30. Part I of Justice Kennedy's Opinion of the Court, joined by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg. All nine directly adopt the classification and application. Part II of Justice Kennedy's opinion, joined by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter and Thomas. Eight Justices adopt this additional bounded procedural explanation. Ginsburg joins the common classification and remedy but not this account. Part III of Justice Kennedy's opinion, joined by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg. All nine adopt the jury rule and bounded reversal/remand.

**Present operation effective:** International Union, United Mine Workers of America v. Bagwell, 1994-06-30.

**Exceptions and limits:** Size and complexity alone do not define every contempt. The decision creates no universal numerical seriousness threshold, erases no properly accrued coercive fine automatically, and leaves the distinct procedures for petty and direct contempt outside its holding.

**Holdings navigation:** The surviving fixed public fines are criminal punishment; Necessity for enforcement does not excuse criminal procedure on this record; Serious criminal contempt requires a jury and these civil assessments cannot stand.

### Equitable vacatur after settlement moots review

**Governing question:** Whether mootness from voluntary settlement warrants vacating a judgment lawfully brought for review.

**Current rule:** Subsequent mootness prevents a merits decision but leaves authority under 28 U.S.C. §2106 to make a just disposition of the judgment and proceeding. Voluntary settlement ordinarily does not establish entitlement to vacatur: the movant must supply a further sufficient equitable reason. Exceptional settlement circumstances can warrant relief, but a settlement term requiring vacatur is not itself such a circumstance. Section 2106 permits appropriate relief; it does not command vacatur whenever review becomes moot.

All nine directly adopt this proposition.

Justice Scalia's Opinion of the Court, joined in full by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. All nine directly adopt this proposition.

**Present operation effective:** 1994-11-08; the component authorities identified above.

**Exceptions and limits:** No heightened proof quantum or exhaustive list of exceptional circumstances is adopted. This settlement rule does not turn loss of review through circumstances outside the parties’ control into automatic vacatur.

### State immunity of bistate compact entities

**Governing question:** When a bistate compact entity shares its constituent States’ Eleventh Amendment immunity.

**Current rule:** Exercise of governmental power alone does not confer the States’ immunity. The entity’s actual legal, financial and institutional relationship must give good reason to conclude that the States structured it as their arm and Congress concurred. Exposure of the state treasuries is highly probative but not categorically indispensable; a separate, self-supporting enterprise responsible for its own obligations cannot claim immunity merely from its public functions.

Six of nine participants directly support this entity-specific rule and its application to both employee actions. O'Connor, Scalia and Thomas dissent; no fragmented-rationale analysis is needed.

**Present operation effective:** 1994-11-14; the component authorities identified above.

**Exceptions and limits:** This compact-entity inquiry does not establish a universal sole-treasury test, decide abrogation or consent, or equate immunity with governmental status for constitutional-rights purposes.

**Holdings navigation:** PATH’s actual compact and financial structure does not confer the States’ immunity.

### FEC certiorari authority and timely ratification

**Governing question:** Who may invoke Supreme Court review of an ordinary FECA enforcement action and when later authorization can cure an unauthorized filing.

**Current rule:** The Commission’s general litigation-and-appeal power under §437d(a)(6) does not displace 28 U.S.C. §518(a)’s allocation of Supreme Court representation. The Attorney General may direct otherwise in a particular case; express certiorari authority under 26 U.S.C. §§9010(d) and 9040(d) is confined to actions under those respective funding provisions. Authorization first supplied after the period for an authorized petition has expired cannot relate back to validate an unauthorized invocation. Section 2101(c) allows ninety days, with a Justice permitted for good cause to extend the application period by no more than sixty days.

### Qualified-immunity legal appeals and factual sufficiency

**Governing question:** The boundary of immediate review under §1291 when qualified immunity is denied.

**Current rule:** Immediate review may address the separable legal question whether conduct on the relevant assumed facts violates clearly established law, including the legality of a categorical direct-evidence condition. It may not determine only whether pretrial evidence creates a genuine dispute about the official’s participation, or choose between disputed motive, causation or factual accounts. A legal appeal uses the district court’s assumed facts; if not stated, the appellate court may identify likely assumptions favorable to the nonmovant without deciding truth or reweighing sufficiency. An abstract legal contention does not bring the factual dispute within immediate review. An earlier pleading-stage appeal does not by itself exhaust review of a later summary-judgment order: a separable legal immunity question must independently satisfy the collateral-order conditions. This permits neither repetition of an unchanged ruling nor relitigation of matters resolved by the first mandate. Having to defend a different surviving claim does not itself defeat otherwise authorized claim-specific review, but neither supplies missing authorization nor makes that other claim reviewable.

**Authority by component:**

- Factual sufficiency is not an immediate qualified-immunity appeal: Factual sufficiency is not an immediate qualified-immunity appeal, 1995-06-12. Justice Breyer's opinion of the Court, joined by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg; all nine adopt this bounded rule.
- Separable legal review of the categorical evidence rule: Separable legal review of the categorical evidence rule, 1995-06-12. Ginsburg's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Breyer; all nine support this legal-review proposition.

- Successive-stage review and preserved mandate limits: Behrens — Holding 1, February 21, 1996; Ginsburg Part I for Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and herself (seven).
- Conditional assumed-fact rule: Behrens — Holding 2, February 21, 1996; unanimous Part II. Claim-specific effect of another surviving claim: Holding 3, Part III for all eight Associates; Stone-Zsela does not join. Stevens and Breyer join these conditional rules while opposing authorization of the successive appeal.

**Present operation effective:** Behrens, February 21, 1996; Johnson and Kimberlin retain their original component authority.

**Open question:** Genuinely necessary connected review and a categorical rule for every mixed order remain unresolved. Johnson and Kimberlin use their common entering baseline; neither is treated as earlier same-day law for the other.

**Holdings navigation:** Factual sufficiency is not an immediate qualified-immunity appeal; Separable legal review of the categorical evidence rule; Behrens v. Pelletier, 516 U.S. 299.

### Municipal liability defenses and connected interlocutory review

**Governing question:** Whether an officers’ immunity appeal permits immediate review of a separate municipal liability defense.

**Current rule:** An ordinary municipal liability defense remains effectively reviewable after final judgment and does not acquire immunity from trial through the officers’ immunity. An expressly reserved, tentative final-policymaker ruling also lacks the conclusiveness required by Cohen. The court of appeals may not decide a separate party’s nonappealable defense merely because it is related to a valid immunity appeal and its resolution would save litigation.

**Authority by component:**

### Administrative interest and LHWCA appellate aggrievement

**Governing question:** Independent §921(c) appellate aggrievement and the Director’s distinct respondent role in an existing private-party appeal.

**Current rule:** A general interest in correct administration of the LHWCA does not alone make the Director adversely affected or aggrieved under §921(c) by an employee’s unappealed award. Congress may confer an express review right, and genuine financial or independently statutory injury requires its own analysis; this construction is not categorical governmental incapacity to seek review. The Director, as the Secretary’s representative, may respond under then-effective FRAP 15(a) in an employer’s appeal from a Benefits Review Board order while the private parties preserve a live controversy. That respondent role does not authorize an independent Director appeal based solely on administrative interest.

Justice O'Connor's opinion of the Court, joined in full by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, and Breyer: eight direct rationale votes. Justice Ginsburg concurs in the judgment and agrees with the case-specific statutory result, but does not join this explanation. No fractured-opinion synthesis is needed. 
- Respondent status in a live private-party appeal: Ingalls Shipbuilding v. Director, OWCP — Ingalls Shipbuilding, Inc. v. Director, Office of Workers' Compensation Programs — II. The Director may respond in this private-party review, February 18, 1997; O’Connor, Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer.

**Present operation effective:** Ingalls, February 18, 1997, resolves the bounded respondent-status reservation; Newport News’s March 21, 1995 independent-review limit survives.

### Habeas custody in a continuous consecutive sentence series

**Governing question:** Custody under an earlier conviction after its first consecutive segment has been served.

**Current rule:** A prisoner serving a continuous, unexpired series of consecutive sentences remains in custody under an earlier conviction when invalidating it would advance release from the aggregate term, even though that first segment has been served. This establishes only the custody threshold; procedural gates and the conviction’s merits remain separate.

**Present operation effective:** 1995-05-30; the component authorities identified above.

**Exceptions and limits:** Maleng’s rule for an independently expired sentence survives. Collateral consequences after all custody ends do not supply jurisdiction through this rule.

**Holdings navigation:** Custody under a continuous consecutive series.

### Discretion to stay a declaration-only coverage action

**Governing question:** A federal declaratory action addressing state-law coverage alongside adequate parallel state proceedings.

**Current rule:** Section 2201 and Brillhart permit a reasoned stay of a declaration-only state-law coverage action with adequate parallel state proceedings without Colorado River’s exceptional-circumstances showing. The court must consider the state case’s scope, available defenses, interested and necessary parties and amenability to process. Jurisdiction is retained, allowing resumption if the state case fails to resolve the controversy. The lawful exercise of this discretion receives abuse-of-discretion review, which does not insulate a mistaken legal source or unsupported adequacy assessment.

### Covered removal grounds and the bar on appellate remand review

**Governing question:** When §§1447(c)–(d) bar review, including a removal also invoking bankruptcy jurisdiction.

**Current rule:** A remand to the originating state court for a timely raised removal-procedure defect or lack of subject-matter jurisdiction is not reviewable on appeal or otherwise under §1447(d), even when removal also invokes §1452; a procedural-remand motion must be made within thirty days after removal. The then-applicable exception permits review of a case removed pursuant to §1443. Courts may identify the stated ground but may not review a covered ground's correctness merely because it is alleged erroneous. A Burford abstention remand is outside this bar, but absence of the bar does not itself create an appellate route. Section 1452(b) coexists with the ordinary bar rather than displacing it.

### Appeal of an abstention order surrendering the federal forum

**Governing question:** A remand that completely disassociates the district court from the action.

**Current rule:** Absent a statutory review bar, an abstention remand conclusively surrendering federal adjudication is appealable under §1291 on two independently sufficient grounds: Moses H. Cone's limited effectively-out-of-court finality rule and Cohen's collateral-order rule. The latter requires a conclusive, important federal-forum question separate from the merits and effectively unreviewable after a later federal final judgment; this surrender satisfies each condition. Mere delay, litigation expense or an asserted right to avoid trial does not suffice. Thermtron's mandamus-only language yields to this application of Cone, while its construction of the covered-remand bar survives.

- Independent finality and collateral-order grounds, with limited disavowal: Quackenbush — Complete surrender of the federal forum supplies an appealable decision; The collateral-order doctrine independently permits this appeal, June 3, 1996; unanimous Court opinion.

### Burford abstention and independent legal-damages claims

**Governing question:** Whether abstention permits surrender of an action seeking coercive contract damages.

**Current rule:** Outright dismissal or remand under the governing Burford abstention precedents requires equitable or otherwise discretionary relief; the court may not relinquish independent coercive contract-damages claims. An otherwise justified stay may postpone litigation while preserving federal jurisdiction, but its conditions must separately be satisfied. A declaratory count does not make the entire action declaration-only. Subject to timely and adequate state review, NOPSI's alternative grounds concern difficult state-law questions of substantial public importance transcending the immediate result, or disruption of state efforts to establish coherent policy on a matter of substantial public concern; they are not cumulative requirements, and complexity or possible conflict alone is insufficient.

### Ancillary enforcement and a new judgment debtor

**Governing question:** Whether an existing federal judgment supplies jurisdiction over a later independent action imposing its debt on another person.

**Current rule:** The court's power to identify, preserve and execute against its judgment debtor's assets does not confer jurisdiction over a later independent action imposing that debtor's full obligation on another person. Such an action needs an independent jurisdictional basis; factual connection, remedial need, Rule 69 and a supplemental-jurisdiction claim lacking an original federal anchor cannot supply it. The decree-effectuation branch of ancillary jurisdiction remains distinct from factual interdependence and from creation of a new obligation.

**Present operation effective:** Peacock, February 21, 1996.

**Exceptions and limits:** Ordinary contempt, asset discovery, attachment, garnishment and fraudulent-transfer process directed to debtor property remain available on their own lawful predicates, as does an independently founded action. There is no general bar on every alter-ego proceeding or every proceeding involving a nondebtor, and ancillary subject-matter jurisdiction does not itself authorize nationwide service.

### Recognition of state representative-settlement judgments

**Governing question:** A state class-settlement judgment releasing claims within exclusive federal adjudicatory jurisdiction.

**Current rule:** Section 1738 first requires the effect the rendering State gives its judgment; class form, consent disposition and exclusive federal jurisdiction alone create no categorical exception. Approval of an authorized representative release differs from adjudicating the released federal liability. Exchange Act §27 does not impliedly partially repeal §1738 for this judgment category. An incorporated, affirmed Delaware release has its ordinary state-law effect subject to Delaware's identical-factual-predicate and representative limits; alleged ordinary state-law error does not itself reopen that judgment. Recognition remains subject to constitutional authority to bind absent persons and does not confer state jurisdiction over federal securities liability or authorize coercive interference with federal litigation.

### Constitutional authority to bind absent litigants

**Governing question:** The due-process prerequisite to claim or issue preclusion against a nonparty.

**Current rule:** Identical interests, vigorous advocacy, resources, public importance and fiscal reliance alone do not authorize binding absent persons' own legal rights. Binding requires constitutionally sufficient consent, control, genuine privity, adequate class or representative litigation, or another recognized relationship or special remedial arrangement consistent with due process. Constitutionally inadequate representation is not independently cured by notice, opportunities to object or opt out; notice alone imposes no general duty on strangers to intervene. Issue preclusion, like claim preclusion, requires a lawful basis to bind the person. Genuine representative public-right adjudication and use of precedent in a later case remain distinct from extinguishing a stranger's personal claim.

**Authority by component:**

- Representation independent of notice and exclusion rights: Matsushita — Constitutional representation and unresolved review questions limit the remand, February 27, 1996; unanimous Part IV-A; eight Associates reserve complete collateral-review scope in IV-B.
- Nonparty binding and direct personal tax claims, including the issue-preclusion alternative: Richards — Holdings II–IV, June 10, 1996; Stone-Zsela for all nine.

**Present operation effective:** Richards, June 10, 1996; Matsushita supplies the retained representation component.

**Open question:** The Court assumes without deciding whether adequate representation may cure absent notice in some representative proceedings. It neither requires individual notice in every such action nor constitutionalizes every federal class-action requirement. The broader adequacy of officials' representation of constituents, ordinary state-law-error review and Matsushita's collateral-review boundary are not resolved.

**Holdings navigation:** Matsushita Electric Industrial Co. v. Epstein, 516 U.S. 367; Richards v. Jefferson County, 517 U.S. 793.

### State compensation limits within federal new-trial review

**Governing question:** The measure and allocation of compensatory-excessiveness review in a New York diversity action.

**Current rule:** The district court applies CPLR §5501(c)'s material-deviation-from-reasonable-compensation measure through Rule 59, retaining federal new-trial procedure and allocation of functions. Pertinent state decisions guide compensation, without fixed prices or an imported state appellate hierarchy. The court of appeals reviews for abuse of discretion, independently correcting legal error and deferring to the district judge's supported case-specific assessment; the Seventh Amendment permits that bounded review but forbids a first-instance appellate valuation of jury-tried compensation. A remittitur must offer the plaintiff reduced recovery or a new jury trial, not simply impose a substituted amount; federal additur remains forbidden.

- Trial/appellate allocation and lawful remittitur: the same Record, Holding II; Souter Part II for the same coalition except Stevens (six).

**Present operation effective:** Gasperini, June 24, 1996.

**Exceptions and limits:** This does not transplant every outcome-affecting state procedure, adopt a fixed damages cap or authorize a conditional increase under state practice. No damages amount follows from the rule.

### Service timing in Suits in Admiralty Act actions

**Governing question:** Whether §742 supplies a separate jurisdictional or procedural deadline alongside Rule 4.

**Current rule:** Section 742's forthwith-service timetable is a procedural direction implementing existing consent, not an independent jurisdictional condition. In a timely commenced domestic SAA action, Congress's later enactment of former Rule 4(j) displaces the inconsistent shorter timetable; the applicable Rule 4 timing scheme and authorized enlargement govern without enlarging substantive consent or removing designated-recipient requirements. Former Rule 4(j) required dismissal without prejudice after notice when service exceeded 120 days without good cause, except foreign service under former subdivision (i). Amended Rule 4(m) requires, after notice, dismissal without prejudice or an order for service within a specified time; good cause requires extension, while enlargement without good cause is permitted but not compelled. Foreign service under (f) and (j)(1) is excepted; a limitations bar may support discretion but does not mandate relief.

**Authority by component:**

- Procedural classification, later-enactment displacement and distinct Rule schemes: Henderson — Holdings I–III, May 20, 1996; Scalia for Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer and himself (seven).

**Present operation effective:** Henderson, May 20, 1996.

**Effective transition:** Amended Rule 4 took effect December 1, 1993 for new cases and, insofar as just and practicable, proceedings then pending. It does not automatically relabel completed 1993 service acts or validate a particular enlargement.

**Exceptions and limits:** The two-year commencement limit and substantive waiver remain. This is no general rule displacing every service statute and no independently sufficient Court-promulgation ground under §2072; the operative conflict is with Congress's direct enactment.

**Holdings navigation:** Henderson v. United States, 517 U.S. 654.

### Grant, vacatur and remand after a material development

**Governing question:** When a changed premise warrants reconsideration without a Supreme Court merits decision.

**Current rule:** Under §2106, an intervening or sufficiently recent development makes grant, vacatur and remand potentially appropriate when there is a reasonable probability that the lower decision rests on a premise that court would reject on reconsideration and reconsideration may affect the ultimate outcome. The Court must independently weigh finality, lower-court independence, delay, cost and manipulative litigation. Government advocacy alone does not justify vacatur. The receiving court decides the development's relevance, authority and effect and may reach the same result; reconsideration establishes neither merits error nor entitlement to relief.

**Authority by component:**

- Probability and independent equities: Lawrence — A material agency development can justify reconsideration without a merits decision, January 8, 1996; per curiam for Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer (six). Stone-Zsela's reasonable-possibility formulation is noncontrolling.

**Present operation effective:** Lawrence, January 8, 1996.

**Exceptions and limits:** No automatic deference to a changed agency view, automatic relief upon Government concession, or conclusive presumption of error from an unexplained judgment is created. Stutson's same-day procedural disposition does not expand Pioneer beyond its decided scope.

**Holdings navigation:** Lawrence v. Chater, 516 U.S. 163.

### Prison-conditions prospective relief

**Governing question:** The original §3626 scope, necessity findings and preliminary-relief conditions.

**Current rule:** In a civil proceeding arising under federal law concerning conditions of confinement or officials' effects on confined persons' lives, prospective relief must be narrowly drawn, extend no further than necessary to correct the particular plaintiffs' federal-right violation and be the least intrusive necessary means; the court must make those findings and give substantial weight to adverse public-safety and criminal-justice-system effects. Relief requiring or permitting an official to exceed state or local authority or otherwise violate that law also requires federal permission, necessity to correct the federal violation and absence of any other corrective relief. The statute confers no authority to build prisons or raise taxes and preserves otherwise applicable remedial limits.

Otherwise authorized preliminary injunctive relief must be narrow, no broader than necessary for the identified harm and least intrusive, with substantial safety/system weight and respect for the distinct state-law conditions. It expires ninety days after entry unless the court makes the prospective-relief findings and makes the order final before expiration. An existing permanent decree does not automatically become a preliminary order.

**Authority by component:**

- Enacted conditions, scope and all-relief transition: PLRA §§802–804 — Source, authority and operative text, §802, original 18 U.S.C. §3626(a)(1)–(2), (c)–(d), (g) and §802(b)(1), April 26, 1996.
- Existing-decree application and substantive findings: Lewis v. Casey — Holdings IV–VI, Holding IV, June 24, 1996; Kennedy Part IV for all eight Associates; Stone-Zsela joins only the statutory disposition. 
- Bounded constitutional operation of termination, not a change to the present entry’s remedial conditions: Plyler v. Moore, Plyler v. Moore — II. The prospective-relief rule preserves judicial adjudication, June 23, 1997; see the termination entry’s component authority.

**Present operation effective:** PLRA, April 26, 1996; Lewis v. Casey, June 24, 1996, supplies the controlling application and qualifications.

**Controlling construction:** Prospective relief is all relief other than compensatory monetary damages. A §3626 civil prison-conditions action excludes habeas proceedings challenging the fact or duration of confinement. A prison includes federal, state and local juvenile or adult criminal detention facilities. Consent decrees include relief based wholly or partly on consent or acquiescence and must comply with subsection (a). Private settlements whose only federal judicial enforcement is reinstatement of the settled proceeding are distinct; otherwise available state breach remedies survive. Section 3626 does not govern relief a state court enters solely on state-law claims.

**Effective transition:** Amended §3626 applies to prospective relief originally granted or approved before, on or after April 26, 1996. Existing findings may meet the necessary predicates at their actual scope; ritual wording, modest cost or reasonableness alone neither establishes nor defeats compliance. Prison-conditions termination motions and automatic stays states Plyler’s June 23, 1997 resolution of the presented Article III and due-process objections to original §3626(b)(2), with the full §3626(b)(3) preservation condition. Other constitutional objections remain unresolved.

**Related current rules:** Prison-conditions termination motions and automatic stays states the separate actual-motion triggers; Prisoner-release orders and prison crowding supplies additional release-order requirements.

**Holdings navigation:** Lewis v. Casey, 518 U.S. 343 (1996). Plyler v. Moore (1997-06-23) — Federal Courts / Prison access and prospective relief.

### Prisoner-release orders and prison crowding

**Governing question:** Orders whose purpose or effect reduces or limits prison population or directs release or nonadmission.

**Current rule:** A prisoner-release order in a civil prison-conditions action requires a prior less intrusive order that failed to remedy the federal-right deprivation and a reasonable opportunity for the defendant to comply. In federal court only a three-judge court convened under §2284 may enter such relief, and only on clear and convincing evidence that crowding is the primary cause of the violation and no other relief will remedy it. A requesting party must request the three-judge court and supply material establishing the antecedent failed-relief and compliance-time predicates. Once those predicates exist, the district judge may also request a three-judge court on the judge's own initiative if a release order should be considered.

A state or local official or governmental unit with functions covering appropriations for construction, operation or maintenance of program facilities, or prosecution or custody of those affected by release or nonadmission, may oppose imposition or continuation, seek termination and intervene. Temporary and preliminary population-reducing orders fall within the release-order definition; their label supplies no exemption.

**Authority by component:**

- Release-order definition, predicates, burden, procedure and participation: PLRA §§802–804 — Source, authority and operative text, §802, original §3626(a)(3), (g)(4), April 26, 1996.

**Present operation effective:** PLRA, April 26, 1996.

**Related current rules:** Prison-conditions prospective relief supplies the independently required scope, findings, definitions and transition. Enactment proves neither crowding nor failure of prior relief and orders no prisoner's release.

### Prison-conditions termination motions and automatic stays

**Governing question:** When existing prospective relief becomes terminable or stayed under original §3626.

**Current rule:** On a party's or intervener's motion, prospective prison-conditions relief is terminable two years after grant or approval, one year after denial of a termination motion under §3626(b)(1), or, for an order on or before enactment, two years after April 26, 1996. A defendant or intervener is entitled to immediate termination when relief was entered without the required need, narrowness and least-intrusiveness findings. Relief shall not terminate if the court makes written, record-based findings that it remains necessary to correct a current OR ongoing federal-right violation and is narrowly drawn, no broader than necessary and least intrusive. Earlier agreed modification or termination and otherwise lawful earlier judicial modification or termination remain possible.

The court must promptly decide modification or termination motions. Under original §3626(e), prospective relief subject to an actual pending motion is automatically stayed from day thirty after filing a motion under (b)(1) or (b)(2), or day 180 for a motion under other law, until entry of the final order deciding it. Enactment alone creates neither a termination nor an automatic stay.

Section 3626(b)(2) is an independent statutory route: the State must establish its termination predicate, and the court must independently apply the full original (b)(3) preservation condition. Rufo's equitable changed-circumstances threshold is not an additional prerequisite. Existing substantive findings can satisfy the statute without ritual wording. Necessary corrective relief may extend beyond the minimum substantive conduct rule, but negotiated decree terms do not thereby become independent federal rights preserving every obligation. Applied with these safeguards, the rule changes prospective governing law without displacing Article III adjudication or promising beneficiaries perpetual enforcement of unchanged terms. Courts still determine actual violations, findings, necessity and scope; the statute supplies no legislative finding of compliance or permission to cancel accrued damages.

Moore — II. Conditional termination changes governing law without displacing Article III adjudication, Plyler v. Moore — III. Negotiated decree protections are not automatically independent federal rights and Plyler v. Moore — IV. The presented due-process claim does not bar termination, Kennedy for all nine, 1997-06-23.

**Present operation effective:** PLRA, 1996-04-26, with Lewis's 1996-06-24 qualifications and Plyler's 1997-06-23 independent-route and constitutional constructions.

**Related current rules:** Prison-conditions prospective relief defines the covered relief, settlements and all-relief transition. No present qualifying motion or elapsed period is inferred from the statutory rule.

Negotiated decree protections are not automatically independent federal rights; Plyler v. Moore (1997-06-23) — IV. The presented due-process claim does not bar termination.

### Special masters in federal prison-conditions remedies

**Governing question:** Appointment, work and continued use of a statutory master in the remedial phase.

**Current rule:** A master must be disinterested and objective, give due regard to public safety and be warranted by a finding that the remedial phase is sufficiently complex. If appointment is necessary, the institution and plaintiffs each submit up to five names, each side may strike up to three from the other list, and the court selects from those remaining; a party has an interlocutory appeal on partiality. Compensation cannot exceed the §3006A appointed-counsel hourly rate plus reasonably incurred costs, paid from Judiciary appropriations.

The court reviews continuing need every six months. Authorized hearings and proposed findings must be on the record; ex parte findings and communications are prohibited. A master may assist development of remedial plans and may be removed at any time, but must leave when relief terminates. A person exercising a master's powers under Rule 53 or inherent authority is covered regardless of title.

**Authority by component:**

- Appointment, payment, appeal and work requirements: PLRA §§802–804 — Source, authority and operative text, §802, original §3626(f), (g)(8), April 26, 1996.
- Continued remedial use, actual function and accrued-work limits: Lewis v. Casey — Holdings IV–VI, Holding VI, June 24, 1996; all eight Associates join Kennedy Part IV.

**Present operation effective:** PLRA, April 26, 1996; Lewis v. Casey, June 24, 1996, supplies the controlling continued-use qualification.

**Open question:** Accrued fees and particular temporal questions require their own lawful determination; the requirements do not retrospectively invalidate every prior act or fee or establish misconduct.

**Related current rules:** Prison-conditions prospective relief supplies the covered-action and transition provisions.

**Holdings navigation:** Lewis v. Casey, 518 U.S. 343 (1996).

### Statutory exhaustion and screening of prisoner conditions actions

**Governing question:** The original §1997e prefiling condition and distinct screening commands.

**Current rule:** A confined prisoner may not bring a prison-conditions action under §1983 or any other federal law until available administrative remedies are exhausted. On its own motion or a party's motion, the court shall dismiss such an action if satisfied that it is frivolous, malicious, fails to state a claim or seeks money from an immune defendant. A claim that on its face has one of those four defects may be dismissed without first requiring exhaustion. State failure to adopt or adhere to an administrative grievance procedure alone supplies no action under CRIPA §3 or §5. “Prisoner” in §1997e means a person incarcerated or detained in any facility who is accused of, convicted of, sentenced for, or adjudicated delinquent for violations of criminal law or terms or conditions of parole, probation, pretrial release or a diversionary program.

**Authority by component:**

- Available-remedies command, screening and its prior-exhaustion exception: PLRA §§802–804 — Source, authority and operative text, §803(d), original 42 U.S.C. §1997e(a)–(c), (h), April 26, 1996.

**Present operation effective:** PLRA, April 26, 1996.

**Effective transition:** The statute was enacted April 26, 1996. Section 802's express all-prospective-relief transition is not generalized to §1997e or §1915; disputed application to pending matters remains unresolved unless an applicable authority separately resolves it.

**Unresolved interaction:** McCarthy's former damages-only BOP conclusion rested on absence of a statutory command. It supplies no exception to this new text. The admission establishes no litigant's exhaustion or availability finding and adopts no later construction of what makes a remedy available. §1915's fee-screening mechanisms remain distinct.

### Prisoner filing fees, costs and prior dismissal restrictions

**Governing question:** The original §1915 civil-filing requirements and distinct no-assets safeguard.

**Current rule:** A prisoner seeking to bring a civil action or appeal a civil judgment or proceeding without prepayment must supply the asset affidavit and a certified institutional account statement covering the preceding six months from each confining institution. For a covered civil action or in-forma-pauperis appeal, the prisoner owes the full filing fee; when funds exist the initial installment is twenty percent of the greater of average monthly deposits or average monthly balance for those six months. Thereafter monthly payments equal twenty percent of the preceding month's credited income; the custodian forwards them each time the account exceeds ten dollars until paid. Collection cannot exceed the statutorily permitted fee. A prisoner may not be barred from bringing a civil action or appealing a civil or criminal judgment solely for having no assets and no means to pay the initial installment.

If a prisoner's judgment includes costs, the full costs ordered must be paid, never more than ordered; original §1915(f)(2)(B) directs payment in the same manner as subsection (a)(2). Under (g), a prisoner may not bring a civil action or appeal a civil judgment or proceeding under §1915 after three or more prior occasions on which, while incarcerated or detained, the prisoner brought a federal action or appeal dismissed as frivolous, malicious or failing to state a claim, unless under imminent danger of serious physical injury. Paid filing, initial-payment inability and the prior-dismissal exception are different questions.

**Authority by component:**

- Documentation, full fees, installments, safeguard, costs and three-dismissal exception: PLRA §§802–804 — Source, authority and operative text, §804(a), (c)–(e), original 28 U.S.C. §1915(a)(1)–(2), (b), (f)–(h), April 26, 1996.

**Present operation effective:** PLRA, April 26, 1996.

**Effective transition:** The statute was enacted April 26, 1996. Section 802's express all-prospective-relief transition is not generalized to §1997e or §1915; disputed application to pending matters remains unresolved unless an applicable authority separately resolves it.

**Controlling construction:** Section 1915(h) defines prisoner as a person incarcerated or detained in any facility accused of, convicted of, sentenced for or adjudicated delinquent for criminal-law violations or violations of parole, probation, pretrial-release or diversionary-program terms. Prior custody when the earlier action was brought is an independent condition; no existing dismissal is automatically classified as qualifying.

**Open question:** The original costs paragraph actually cross-references (a)(2), the documentation provision. This entry preserves that enacted reference without silently substituting (b)(2) or inventing a judicial correction.

### Dismissal and counsel requests under amended §1915

**Governing question:** Screening despite partial or full fee payment and assistance for persons unable to afford counsel.

**Current rule:** Under original amended §1915(e)(2), the court shall dismiss at any time, notwithstanding any filing fee or portion paid, when it determines that the poverty allegation is untrue or the action or appeal is frivolous, malicious, fails to state a claim or seeks monetary relief from an immune defendant. Section 1915(e)(1) permits the court to request an attorney for any person unable to afford counsel; it does not itself compel an appointment or establish eligibility.

**Authority by component:**

- New screening commands and separate counsel discretion: PLRA §§802–804 — Source, authority and operative text, §804(a)(5), original §1915(e), April 26, 1996.

**Present operation effective:** PLRA, April 26, 1996.

**Effective transition:** The statute was enacted April 26, 1996. Section 802's express all-prospective-relief transition is not generalized to §1997e or §1915; disputed application to pending matters remains unresolved unless an applicable authority separately resolves it.

**Unresolved interaction:** Denton construes former discretionary §1915(d). Its irrational-or-wholly-incredible factual standard and nonmerits distinctions are not a holding construing every new mandatory ground or the appellate standard under amended §1915(e). The new enactment does not convert every pleading failure into factual frivolousness.

### Issues within a permitted certified interlocutory order

**Governing question:** Scope of an appeal permitted under 28 U.S.C. §1292(b).

**Current rule:** Once an interlocutory appeal is lawfully permitted under §1292(b), appellate jurisdiction reaches issues fairly included within the certified order, including an anterior issue supplying its premise, rather than only the question formulated for certification. It reaches no unrelated order merely because that order is associated with the lawsuit. The scope rule dispenses with none of the route’s independent certification, timely-application and discretionary-permission requirements.

**Authority by component:**

- Yamaha — Part I, certified-order scope and statutory sequence, 1996-01-09; O’Connor and all seven other Associates (eight); Stone-Zsela agrees only with the disposition.

**Present operation effective:** Yamaha, January 9, 1996.

**Related current rules:** “Interlocutory review of district-court bankruptcy appellate orders” preserves this statutory route in that setting; “Municipal liability defenses and connected interlocutory review” limits unauthorized addition of unrelated collateral-order issues.

**Holdings navigation:** Yamaha Motor Corp., U.S.A. v. Calhoun, 516 U.S. 199.

### Three-judge review of facial challenges to Telecommunications Act Title V

**Governing question:** The judicial channel for a civil facial challenge to Title V of Public Law 104-104 or an amendment or provision of that title.

**Current rule:** A three-judge district court convened under 28 U.S.C. §2284 must hear a covered facial challenge. An interlocutory or final judgment, decree or order of that court holding a covered provision unconstitutional is reviewable as of right by direct Supreme Court appeal filed within twenty days after entry. This route does not extend to every communications dispute, every as-applied challenge, a judgment upholding the provision, or litigation confined to the separate 1992 provisions.

**Authority by component:**

- Challenge and appeal triggers and deadline: Public Law 104-104, Act §561, effective 1996-02-08; admitted noncase text, preserved as distinct from the 1992 review in Denver, statutory review boundary, 1996-06-28.

**Present operation effective:** Public Law 104-104, Act §561, 1996-02-08.

**Holdings navigation:** Denver Area Educational Telecommunications Consortium, Inc. v. FCC; Alliance for Community Media v. FCC, 518 U.S. 727 (1996).

### Relief confined to the established federal conflict

**Governing question:** The scope and continued operation of declarations and injunctions against a state requirement whose conflict with federal law is limited to identified applications.

**Current rule:** Declaratory and injunctive relief must protect the applications in which the federal conflict is established while preserving severable applications for which no conflict has been shown. Confining relief leaves enacted text in place; it does not itself insert an exception or rewrite state law. Prospective protection must track the applicable federal obligation, rather than participation in a federal program alone regardless of later lawful changes. An actual lawful change may support appropriate modification, but hypothetical future change establishes neither a current lapse nor automatic dissolution. Correcting an excessive or erroneous remedial premise must preserve necessary protection independently supported by federal grounds.

**Authority by component:**

- Conflict-specific scope and temporal operation: Relief must follow the established federal conflict and Prospective protection follows the applicable obligation, 1996-03-18; unanimous per curiam.
- Preservation of independent federal grounds when severability error is corrected: II. Correcting severability does not authorize automatic enforcement, 1996-06-17; per curiam joined by Stone-Zsela, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas (five), applying Dalton rather than changing its scope.

**Present operation effective:** Dalton, 1996-03-18.

**Exceptions and limits:** A proved indivisible defect can warrant broader relief; this is no general rule against broad injunctions or new facial-review formula. No Medicaid funding construction or constitutional abortion-funding entitlement follows. Leavitt’s state-law correction does not adjudicate the surviving provision’s independent constitutional validity, authorize automatic enforcement, or require indefinite retention of every part of a decree.

**Holdings navigation:** Dalton v. Little Rock Family Planning Services, 516 U.S. 474; Leavitt v. Jane L..

### No delay-based substitute for statutory habeas dismissal

**Governing question:** Termination of a first personal federal habeas petition through an additional equitable delay sanction.

**Current rule:** A first personal federal habeas petition meeting jurisdictional and pleading requirements may not be terminated solely for delay and litigation purpose through an additional equitable sanction dispensing with the conditions of habeas statutes and Rules. Section 2243’s law-and-justice direction does not authorize that substitute. Rule 9(a) permits dismissal for delay prejudicing the State’s ability to respond unless reasonable diligence could not have disclosed the grounds before prejudice arose; lost execution dates and general finality costs alone do not establish response prejudice, and no five-year presumption was enacted. Other procedural, abuse and claim-insufficiency grounds require their own actual predicates; failed next-friend proceedings cannot be counted as though necessarily prior personal merits petitions. Section 2243 and Rule 4 retain prompt lawful examination, dismissal where nonentitlement plainly appears and otherwise answer or appropriate judicial action, without an automatic writ or evidentiary hearing.

**Authority by component:**

- Source-bound dismissal and Rule 9(a) limits: I. Delay does not supply the asserted additional dismissal sanction, 1996-04-01; Stevens Part I, all nine.

**Present operation effective:** Lonchar, 1996-04-01.

**Effective transition:** Lonchar construed pre-AEDPA law. AEDPA’s enacted filing and successive-application conditions remain distinct and apply when their temporal and substantive predicates are met; the pending-proceeding transition is not decided wholesale.

**Related current rules:** “Equitable delay independently of a habeas procedural bar” governs the separate stay inquiry, which Lonchar preserves even for a first personal petition.

**Holdings navigation:** Lonchar v. Thomas, 517 U.S. 314.

### Interim protection necessary for required habeas process

**Governing question:** Execution that would prevent genuinely required habeas process when lawful expedition cannot complete it.

**Current rule:** When execution would prevent completion of process actually required by governing habeas law and lawful prompt disposition cannot finish in time, the court must provide the interim protection necessary to make that identified opportunity meaningful. It must identify the unfinished legal obligation and the timing need. Filing alone, first-petition status and a capital sentence establish neither. Rule 4 screening, lawful procedural dismissal and expedition remain available; if they permit a lawful disposition in time, the rule supplies no further stay entitlement. It preserves McFarland’s actual opportunity and proved obstruction inquiry and Gomez’s independent equitable considerations.

**Authority by component:**

- Conditional necessary-process protection: III. Protection must preserve genuinely required process when lawful expedition cannot, 1996-04-01; Stevens Part III with Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer (five), Kennedy’s join confined to the necessary opportunity. Stone-Zsela’s judgment support supplies no additional rationale vote.

**Present operation effective:** Lonchar, 1996-04-01.

**Exceptions and limits:** No automatic evidentiary hearing, merits adjudication, stay period or indefinite continuation follows. A successive-petition stay still requires substantial grounds upon which relief might be granted. Barefoot’s initial certified appeal and certiorari-stage standards retain their separate triggers. Genuinely applicable AEDPA requirements, including qualified chapter 154, are not bypassed.

**Holdings navigation:** Lonchar v. Thomas, 517 U.S. 314.

### Civil-forfeiture defense access despite related criminal absence

**Governing question:** Use of inherent fugitive-disentitlement power to strike timely claims and defenses in civil forfeiture.

**Current rule:** When the court controls the forfeiture property and can enforce its eventual judgment, failure to return for a related criminal prosecution alone does not justify striking timely civil-forfeiture claims and defenses. Inherent authority must reasonably respond to the actual litigation need. Anticipated misuse is not an established violation or inevitable inability to adjudicate. Supported management under statutes, Rules and bounded inherent authority remains available with each source’s predicate, notice, process and justified scope, without a universal exhaustion sequence or least-restrictive-means requirement. Under §881(i), a qualifying federal drug indictment/information, or state/local charge chargeable under those federal provisions, requires a stay of a related §881 action upon Government motion and good cause; each condition is separate. Supported Rule 26(c) discovery protection, proper proof controls and sanctions for actual noncompliance remain possible, including dismissal where Rules 37/41(b) or bounded inherent authority properly support it.

**Authority by component:**

- Inherent-power boundary: I. The asserted inherent power does not support this complete defense bar; conditional lawful management: II. Lawful management and properly supported sanctions remain available, 1996-06-10; Scalia’s unanimous opinion.

**Present operation effective:** Degen, 1996-06-10.

**Exceptions and limits:** This is an inherent-power holding, not a decision whether Congress could constitutionally authorize a different bar. Criminal appellate disentitlement retains its own scope. Restoration of a defense opportunity establishes no entitlement to the property or automatic indefinite stay.

### One-year state-custody habeas filing period

**Governing question:** The limitation period under amended §2244(d).

**Current rule:** A person in custody pursuant to a state-court judgment has one year to apply for habeas relief, running from the latest of: finality by completion of direct review or expiration of time to seek it; removal of a State-created filing impediment violating federal law that actually prevented filing; initial Supreme Court recognition of the asserted constitutional right, if newly recognized and made retroactively applicable on collateral review; or when due diligence could have discovered the claim’s factual predicate. Time during which a properly filed application for state postconviction or other collateral review of the pertinent judgment or claim is pending is excluded.
